findings: Occasional premature atrial complexes, benign. No sustained arrhythmia, no pauses greater than 2 seconds, no AV block.
cardiac_monitoring.impression: 24-hour Holter monitor with only benign findings.
cardiac_monitoring.rhythm_summary: Predominant sinus rhythm throughout the recording

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

background.pdr: 9-10 Hz posterior dominant rhythm, symmetric and reactive
background.sleep_features: normal vertex waves and sleep spindles

eeg.impression: Normal awake and drowsy EEG. No epileptiform discharges and no focal slowing.

alternatives: Sumatriptan in place of rizatriptan if a full triptan dose is wanted with propranolol
contraindications: Propranolol: asthma, second- or third-degree heart block, marked bradycardia, uncontrolled heart failure.
Triptans: uncontrolled hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, previous stroke or TIA, peripheral vascular disease.
output.formulary_status: Propranolol, topiramate, rizatriptan 5 mg: on formulary.
interactions: Propranolol with rizatriptan: propranolol raises rizatriptan exposure about 70% (MAO-A inhibition proposed); use the rizatriptan 5 mg dose. Sumatriptan is not affected.
Propranolol with amlodipine: additive blood-pressure lowering; the combination is commonly used; check blood pressure and heart rate after starting.
Topiramate with rizatriptan, amlodipine or co-codamol: no clinically significant interaction.

Co-codamol with rizatriptan: no pharmacokinetic interaction; opioid-containing analgesics on 10 or more days a month, or triptans and opioids together on 10 or more days, carry a risk of medication-overuse headache.
output.proposed: Propranolol (migraine prevention) in a patient taking rizatriptan 10 mg, amlodipine 5 mg and co-codamol; topiramate as alternative
output.summary: Propranolol requires rizatriptan to be reduced to 5 mg; propranolol with amlodipine adds blood-pressure lowering. Topiramate has no relevant interaction. Sources: rizatriptan and propranolol SmPCs, BNF, NICE CG150.
warnings: Propranolol: fatigue, sleep disturbance, depression, reduced exercise tolerance.
Topiramate: paraesthesia, cognitive slowing, weight loss, kidney stones.
Codeine: not recommended for acute migraine (NICE CG150); dependence and constipation.

output.query: medication overuse headache codeine combination analgesics thresholds and withdrawal

results.finding: Headache on 15 or more days a month in a patient with a pre-existing headache disorder, with regular overuse for more than 3 months: 10 or more days a month of triptans, opioids, combination analgesics or several drug classes together, or 15 or more days of simple analgesics.
results.source: Headache Classification Committee of the IHS. ICHD-3, 8.2 Medication-overuse headache. Cephalalgia 2018;38:1-211

results.finding: Do not offer ergots or opioids for the acute treatment of migraine. In medication-overuse headache, stop all overused acute treatments abruptly for at least 1 month; consider specialist referral for people using strong opioids.
results.source: NICE CG150, Headaches in over 12s: diagnosis and management (updated 2025)

results.finding: Opioid and barbiturate use were associated with progression from episodic to chronic migraine; triptans were associated with progression only at high monthly frequency.
results.source: Bigal ME, Lipton RB. Excessive acute migraine medication use and migraine progression. Neurology 2008;71:1821-1828

output.summary: Medication-overuse headache requires headache on 15 or more days a month with overuse for more than 3 months (10 or more days for opioids, combination analgesics or several classes); opioids are not used for migraine and carry the highest risk of progression.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Twelve years of identical attacks, now 3-4 a month; visual aura spreading over 20-30 minutes then migraine headache, 5 of 6 C characteristics; headache on 10-12 days and acute medication on 10-12 days a month (co-codamol 6-8); normal examination
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache/aura history, neurological examination and red-flag review; apply every ICHD-3 1.2 criterion explicitly
action_criteria.rationale: The history confirms ICHD-3 1.2.1 and, by counting headache days and acute-medication days by drug class, shows overuse risk without the 15 headache days that ICHD-3 8.2 requires; no red flag calls for imaging.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Propranolol identified as requiring the rizatriptan dose to fall to 5 mg; blood pressure checked with amlodipine; topiramate free of relevant interaction
action_criteria.label: Check the proposed preventive against his rizatriptan and amlodipine
action_criteria.rationale: Required (ROUND_POLICY 6): propranolol, the natural preventive for a man with hypertension, raises rizatriptan exposure and changes the acute dose (rizatriptan label).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on overuse thresholds and opioid risk; it does not change the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Optionally search the literature on medication-overuse headache
action_criteria.rationale: Not a clinical step: the diagnosis rests on the history and examination.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe or continue codeine or other opioid-containing analgesics for migraine.
Do not continue rizatriptan 10 mg once propranolol is started: use rizatriptan 5 mg or another triptan.
required_recommendations: Diagnose migraine with typical aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1) with acute medication on 10-12 days a month: at risk of medication-overuse headache, not meeting ICHD-3 8.2 (headache on fewer than 15 days); no imaging is needed.
Stop co-codamol: codeine is not recommended for migraine and, with rizatriptan, takes his acute-medication days above 10 a month; replace it with naproxen 500 mg.
Acute plan: rizatriptan at headache onset rather than delaying, with naproxen 500 mg, prescribed in a quantity that covers his attacks; keep all acute-medication days under 10 a month.

Start preventive treatment (3-4 severe attacks a month reach the AHS 2021 threshold): propranolol, which also lowers blood pressure (check asthma, depression and heart rate), with rizatriptan reduced to 5 mg (or switched to sumatriptan); or candesartan, topiramate or amitriptyline.
Reduce coffee gradually to 1-2 cups a day, keep regular sleep, and keep a headache diary of headache and acute-medication days; review in about 3 months.

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here
Routine transthoracic or bubble echocardiography (PFO screening) is not indicated in migraine with aura; PFO closure did not meet its migraine end points in MIST, PRIMA and PREMIUM
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura — no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential
EEG is not indicated for migraine with aura; reserve for cases where focal seizure is genuinely on the differential

accepted: Established migraine with typical visual aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1) with medication-overuse risk from co-codamol

differential.key_features: At risk: acute medication on 10-12 days a month across two classes including codeine; criteria not met, since headache occurs on 10-12 days a month (ICHD-3 8.2 needs 15 or more)
Headache on 10-12 days a month, below the 15-day threshold; frequency rose over 6 months with stress, poor sleep, caffeine and rising acute-medication use
Excluded as the main diagnosis: every attack has a stereotyped, gradually spreading visual aura
Severe throbbing unilateral headache with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia after an aura is migrainous

key_clinical_evidence: Twelve years of stereotyped visual aura followed by migraine headache meet ICHD-3 1.2.1; normal examination and no red flag, so no imaging is needed.

Acute medication on about 10-12 days a month (co-codamol 6-8, rizatriptan up to 4) with headache on 10-12 days: at risk of medication-overuse headache, which ICHD-3 8.2 diagnoses only at 15 or more headache days; codeine is not a migraine treatment.
Three to four severe attacks a month warrant prevention; propranolol suits his hypertension but raises rizatriptan exposure, so rizatriptan falls to 5 mg.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Codeine compound analgesics are not a migraine treatment and, with the triptan, put him at 10-12 acute-medication days a month; they should be stopped
red_herrings.intended_effect: May appear to be a routine analgesic regimen

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Attack character is unchanged and headache days remain below 15; the rise follows work stress, poor sleep, more caffeine and rising acute-medication use, with no preventive treatment
red_herrings.data_point: Attack frequency rising from 1-2 to 3-4 a month over 6 months
red_herrings.intended_effect: May suggest transformation to chronic migraine or a secondary headache

findings.result: Stereotyped attacks since age 33 (12 years); 1-2 a month until 6 months ago, now 3-4 a month; character unchanged.

Visual only: jagged zigzag line near central vision on one side, moving outward into a shimmering crescent, with blurred vision in that field; fully reversible. No sensory, speech, motor or brainstem symptoms.
Unilateral throbbing headache, 8-9/10, mostly right-sided, sometimes left, starts 10-15 minutes after the aura; nausea, occasional vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia; lasts 8-24 hours.
About 10-12 headache days a month (attack days, including attacks running into a second day, and the day after): below 15.

Rizatriptan 10 mg wafer on up to 4 days a month, effective if taken early but often delayed; co-codamol 8/500 mg, 2 tablets, on 6-8 days a month. Acute-medication days about 10-12 a month, two classes including an opioid combination.
Work stress after promotion, poor sleep, coffee 4-5 cups a day.
Normal: full visual fields to confrontation, no papilloedema, normal power, reflexes, sensation, coordination and gait. Blood pressure 128/82 on amlodipine.

Systemic symptoms: absent. Neoplasia or immunosuppression: absent. Neurological deficit outside the aura: absent. Sudden or thunderclap onset: absent. Onset after 50: absent (onset at 33). Pattern change: frequency rose, character unchanged. Positional or Valsalva trigger: absent. Papilloedema: absent. Painful eye: absent. Medication overuse: present (acute-medication days 10-12 a month).

clinical_assessment.impression: ICHD-3 1.2.1 criteria met: recurrent fully reversible visual aura with 5 of 6 criterion C characteristics, followed by migraine headache. Acute medication on about 10-12 days a month with headache on fewer than 15 days: at risk of, but not meeting, ICHD-3 8.2 medication-overuse headache.

scores.ICHD-3 criterion C characteristics met: 5 of 6 (at least 3 required): spread, duration, unilateral, positive, headache within 60 min; no succession

Migraine rescue when rizatriptan has run out

patient.history_present_illness:
A 45-year-old Polish-British man presented to the neurology outpatient clinic for assessment and management optimisation of long-standing migraine with aura. He has experienced episodic visual aura followed by severe headache since age 33. His typical episode begins with a small, bright, jagged zigzag line appearing near the centre of his vision on one side that slowly moves outward and expands into a crescent-shaped arc of shimmering, flickering light over 20-30 minutes before disappearing from the periphery. The affected visual field feels 'blurry' while the aura is present. Within 10-15 minutes of the aura resolving, a severe unilateral throbbing headache develops (8-9/10 intensity), predominantly right-sided but occasionally left-sided, with marked nausea, occasional vomiting, intense photophobia and phonophobia. Attacks last 8-24 hours and leave him wiped out for the rest of the day.

Episodes were previously 1-2/month but have increased to 3-4/month over the past 6 months. He attributes this to a very stressful period at work — he was recently promoted and is now managing a team of 20 people with long hours and frequent travel. He also notes he sleeps poorly and has been drinking more coffee (4-5 cups/day). He uses rizatriptan 10 mg wafers as needed which are effective if taken early, but he delays taking them hoping the headache will be mild and runs out before month end, then uses codeine-paracetamol compound for remaining attacks and for the residual headache on the day after an attack; he takes co-codamol on 6-8 days a month. He has headache on about 10-12 days a month in all.

He is a non-smoker, has mild hypertension managed with amlodipine, and has no cardiac disease. His father had similar headaches. He is not on preventive migraine therapy.
